prompts.L4:

A surreal speaker encounters a sad-eyed man who has locked his head in a Japanese box, and their exchange uses dreamlike imagery and dialogue to explore sadness, perception, memory, and selfhood. The two figures recognize themselves in each other and imaginatively merge within the painted scene, suggesting that art and storytelling can preserve life, identity, and connection “as if” they were alive.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Sarah, The, Gillyflowers

outputs.L1:
(For Sarah, when she is older)

The round, sad-eyed man puffed cigars as if he were alive. Gillyflowers stood to the left of the apple, purple bells to the right, and a grass-covered hill rose behind.

“I am sad today,” said the sad-eyed man, “for I have locked my head in a Japanese box and lost the key. I am sad today,” he told me, “for there are gillyflowers by the apple and purple bells I cannot see. Will you look at them for me,” he asked, “and tell me what you find?”

“I cannot,” I replied, “for my eyes have grown sugary and dim from reading too long by candlelight.”

“Then tell me what you have read,” said the round, sad-eyed man.

“I cannot,” I replied, “for my memory has grown tired and dim from looking at things that cannot be seen by any kind of light. And I, too, have locked my head in a Japanese box and thrown away the key.”

“Then I am you, and you are me,” said the sad-eyed man, as if alive. “I’ll write you in where I should be—between the gillyflowers and the purple bells, the apple and the hill—and we’ll puff cigars from noon till night, as if we were alive.”
outputs.L2:
(for Sarah, years from now)

The plump man with mournful eyes smoked cigars with the strange conviction of someone living. On one side of the apple stood gillyflowers; on the other, purple bell-shaped blossoms, and beyond them rose a hill carpeted with grass.

“I am unhappy today,” said the sorrowful-eyed man, “because I shut my head inside a Japanese box and misplaced the key.”

“I am unhappy today,” he said to me, “because gillyflowers grow near the apple, and purple bells are there too, but I cannot see them.”

“Will you see them on my behalf,” he asked, “and tell me what is there?”

“I can’t,” I answered, “because my eyes have turned sweetened and clouded from too many hours reading by candle flame.”

“Then tell me what you have been reading,” said the round man with the sad eyes.

“I can’t,” I said, “because my memory has become weary and hazy from staring at things no light can reveal. Besides, I too have sealed my head inside a Japanese box and tossed the key away.”

“Then I am you, and you are me,” said the sad-eyed man, in the manner of someone alive. “I’ll put you down in the place where I ought to stand, among the gillyflowers, the purple bells, the apple, and the hill, and together we’ll smoke cigars from midday until dark, as though we were living.”
outputs.L3:
The sad-eyed man appears as a strange, almost dreamlike figure, surrounded by gillyflowers, purple bells, an apple, and a hill covered with grass. Everything around him seems vivid and symbolic, as though he belongs less to the ordinary world than to a surreal landscape shaped by feeling and imagination.

He explains that he is sad because he has locked his head inside a Japanese box and has lost the key. This odd confession suggests a deeper kind of imprisonment: his thoughts, identity, or ability to understand himself have been shut away somewhere he can no longer reach. His sadness comes not only from loss, but from being separated from his own mind.

The man then asks the narrator to look at the flowers for him. However, the narrator cannot do this, because their eyes have grown dim from reading by candlelight. The request reveals the man’s dependence on another person’s vision, while the narrator’s response shows their own exhaustion and limitation. Even the act of seeing has become difficult.

The narrator also admits that they cannot remember what they have read. Their memory has been worn down by the effort of trying to perceive things that cannot be seen. This suggests a life spent searching for hidden meanings, invisible truths, or experiences beyond ordinary perception. In trying to understand what lies beyond sight, the narrator has lost touch with what was once clearly known.

In the end, the sad-eyed man and the narrator recognize something of themselves in one another. Each is marked by loss, limitation, and a longing to perceive or recover what has been taken away. They imagine sharing the same place “as if they were alive,” creating a fragile sense of companionship in a world that feels suspended between reality, memory, and dream.
outputs.L4:
A surreal speaker encounters a sad-eyed man who has locked his own head inside a Japanese box, as though he has tried to hide his thoughts from the world or preserve them like a delicate object. The scene unfolds with the logic of a dream: objects seem symbolic, space feels painted rather than solid, and the conversation between the two figures moves between ordinary speech and strange, luminous imagery. The man’s sadness is not explained in a direct or realistic way; instead, it appears through the box, through his eyes, through the atmosphere around him, and through the speaker’s attempts to understand what he sees.

As they speak, the encounter becomes less about one person observing another and more about the unstable boundary between them. The speaker looks at the man and begins to recognize something familiar in his sorrow, his confinement, and his fractured sense of self. The man, in turn, seems to reflect the speaker back to himself. Their dialogue explores how perception shapes identity: what one sees in another person may also be a hidden part of oneself. Memory, sadness, and imagination overlap until it becomes unclear whether the man is a separate figure, a figure in a painting, a remembered self, or an invention made real by the act of looking.

Gradually, the two figures seem to merge inside the painted world that contains them. The Japanese box, the sad eyes, and the dreamlike surroundings become part of a shared inner landscape. Rather than resolving the mystery, the text suggests that art does not need to explain life in order to preserve it. Through image, story, and imagination, the speaker and the man remain connected “as if” they were alive. The phrase implies both illusion and survival: art cannot fully restore the living person, but it can hold a version of life, feeling, and identity in suspension. In this way, the encounter becomes a meditation on how storytelling allows sadness to be seen, how the self may be discovered in another, and how art can keep human connection alive beyond ordinary limits.
outputs.L5:
**Sarah and The Gillyflowers**

Sarah had always loved the quiet corner of the garden where the gillyflowers grew. Their soft, sweet scent drifted through the air each morning, reminding her of warm summers and peaceful afternoons. While the rest of the world hurried by, Sarah liked to sit among the blooms with a book in her lap and sunlight on her shoulders.

The gillyflowers were more than just plants to her. They were a memory of her grandmother, who had planted them years ago and told Sarah that flowers could hold stories if you listened closely enough. So Sarah listened—to the buzzing bees, the rustling leaves, and the gentle whisper of petals in the breeze.

One day, as the sky turned gold at sunset, Sarah noticed a new bloom opening among the gillyflowers. It was brighter than the others, glowing softly in the fading light. She smiled, feeling as though the garden had given her a small gift.

From then on, Sarah visited the gillyflowers every day, caring for them with patience and love. And in return, they filled her world with beauty, fragrance, and the quiet magic of remembering.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, melancholy prose poem in a childlike fairy-tale voice, dedicated “for Sarah when she’s older,” featuring a sad-eyed man, flowers, an apple, a hill, cigars, and a Japanese box.
counterfactuals.output:
**for Sarah when she’s older**

Once there was a sad-eyed man who lived at the bottom of a hill, where the grass grew soft as whispers and the flowers leaned toward him as if he were the last warm window in the world.

Every morning he climbed the hill carrying an apple in one hand and a little Japanese box in the other. The box was painted with cranes and moons and tiny blue waves, and inside it he kept the things he could not say: a button from his mother’s coat, the smell of rain, three paper stars, and the names of people who had gone away.

At the top of the hill he would sit and polish the apple on his sleeve until it shone like a small red planet. Then he would take out a cigar, though he never lit it, because smoke reminded him of ghosts learning to fly. He only held it between his fingers and looked down at the village, where roofs slept like brown animals and children’s voices rose and fell like kites.

The flowers loved him. They grew around his shoes and up through the hems of his trousers. Daisies asked him questions. Poppies told him lies. One violet, very brave and very small, climbed into his pocket and stayed there all winter, dreaming purple dreams.

But the sad-eyed man could not be comforted. Not by the apple. Not by the cigars. Not by the hill, which lifted him closer to heaven every day and still could not make heaven answer.

One evening, when the sky was the color of old peaches, he opened the Japanese box and placed the apple inside. The apple was too large, but the box became bigger in a quiet, polite way, the way magic does when it does not want to frighten a child.

Then he put in the cigars, one by one, and the flowers, and the hill, and the village with its sleeping roofs, and finally his own sad eyes.

After that, nobody saw him again.

But sometimes, Sarah, when you are older and the world has begun to put little stones in your pockets, you may find a painted box waiting where you did not leave it. If you open it gently, you will hear a hill breathing in its sleep. You will smell unlit cigars, and see flowers bowing their heads around a bright apple.

And if you look very closely, you may find the sad-eyed man inside, no bigger than a story, holding out his hand as if to say:

Here is the sorrow.  
Here is the sweetness.  
They were always the same fruit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short piece of whimsical literary nonsense that sounds like it belongs in an illustrated children’s book for adults, with repeated phrases about being “sad today” and someone locking their head in a Japanese box.
counterfactuals.output:
“I am sad today,” said Millicent Moon,  
as she buttered her gloves with a pewter spoon.  
“I am sad today, and the parsnips agree,  
and the clock has been whispering backwards at me.”

So she locked her head in a Japanese box,  
with lacquered moons and impossible locks.  
She tied it up neatly with yesterday’s string,  
then waited to see if her elbows would sing.

“I am sad today,” said the box to the hat.  
“I am sad today,” said the hat to the cat.  
The cat, being wise, merely blinked at the floor  
and posted itself through the crack in the door.

At tea, they all sat where their shadows had been,  
with cups full of thunder and cakes full of tin.  
And still from the box came a small, muffled cry:  
“I am sad today, but I don’t quite know why.”

So they painted the rain with a gooseberry brush,  
and shushed all the spoons with a feathery hush.  
Then Millicent’s head, from its lacquered retreat,  
remarked, “I am sad—but the sadness is sweet.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an eerie, poetic monologue inspired by a strange still-life painting: include gillyflowers, purple bells, an apple, a grass-covered hill, and a round sad-eyed man who may or may not be alive.
counterfactuals.output:
At first I thought the gillyflowers were listening.

They leaned from their cracked blue jug with the patience of old witnesses, petals clotted dark as bruised velvet, their little green throats full of secrets they had not yet decided to breathe. Beside them hung the purple bells, bowed and soundless, as if some invisible hand had rung them once in a room beneath the earth and the echo had never come home.

There was an apple, too—too red, too still—resting where no hand had set it down. Its skin shone with the damp polish of temptation or fever. I could not tell whether it had fallen from a tree, a pocket, or a dream. I only knew it had the look of something that remembers teeth.

Behind all this, improbable and tender, rose a grass-covered hill. Not a landscape, no—more like a thought the painting had tried to bury. The grass grew thick over its rounded back, a small green silence swelling toward the sky. I watched it long enough to fear it might be breathing.

And there, half in front of the hill and half inside it, sat the round sad-eyed man.

His face was pale as dough left too long in moonlight. His cheeks sagged with a softness almost childlike, and his eyes—oh, those eyes—were two wet stones at the bottom of a well. He wore no expression that could be named grief, yet everything in him had already been mourned. His hands rested on his knees, obedient and useless. His mouth was closed as if to keep something from escaping: a word, a moth, a last breath.

I asked him, quietly, whether he was alive.

The gillyflowers did not answer.

The purple bells did not ring.

The apple brightened in its red sleep.

Only the hill seemed to stir beneath its blanket of grass, as though amused by my question—as though life and death were merely colors placed too near each other, bleeding at the edges, making a third thing no one dares to name.

The man’s sad eyes remained fixed on me.

Or perhaps they were painted that way.

Or perhaps I am the one in the painting, and he is waiting, patiently, for me to finish dying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike vignette in the style of Edward Gorey or Donald Barthelme, addressed to a girl named Sarah for when she is older, about memory, sight, sadness, and two figures becoming each other.
counterfactuals.output:
For Sarah, when she is older:

There was once a window that remembered everything placed before it, but only in the rain.

On dry mornings it was merely glass, with a chip in the left corner and the faint breath-mark of someone long gone. But when the rain came down, thin and slant and indecisive, the window showed what had been lost: a blue cup on a sill, a dog turning once in a circle before sleep, a child with a ribbon untied, an old woman closing a book because the ending had found her first.

You, Sarah, will know this window when you see it.

It may be in a house you have never entered, or in a railway carriage passing too slowly through a country that does not admit to having a name. You may be wearing gloves. You may be carrying oranges. You may be sad for no particular reason, which is the saddest kind, since it has nowhere to sit.

Do not look away at once.

At first you will see only yourself, older than you expected and younger than you feel. Your face will hover there, uncertain as a moth. Behind it another face will gather: a girl’s face, pale with attention, her eyes wide from the labor of seeing. She will be watching you as if you were the memory and she the one remembering.

This will be confusing.

“Who are you?” you may ask.

But the rain will answer in its small, grammatical way: *was, was, was.*

The girl will lift her hand. You will lift yours. For a moment the two hands will meet on either side of the glass, not touching, but agreeing to pretend. She will have your sorrow before it was named. You will have her astonishment after it has been used.

Then something peculiar will begin.

Her eyes will become yours. Yours will become hers. The room behind you will fill with toys you do not own and lamps that were thrown away years ago. The room behind her will darken with books, unpaid bills, flowers in a vase leaning toward extinction. You will find yourself remembering things that have not happened to her yet. She will find herself tired from all the days you have already survived.

This is how memory sees: not forward, not backward, but through.

You may be tempted to rescue her. Do not. She is not trapped. Or rather, she is trapped only as everyone is trapped—in the amber of having once been visible.

You may be tempted to apologize. You may say, “I am sorry for the sadness.”

She will not understand. She will think sadness is a large black bird that has landed in the next room, and that if she is very quiet it may go away.

Tell her nothing.

Instead, stand there until the rain blurs both your faces into one. Stand there until the window no longer knows which side is childhood and which is after. Stand there until you are the girl looking out, and the girl is the woman looking in, and each of you is tenderly frightened by the other.

Then the rain will stop.

The window will become ordinary again.

You will go on carrying the oranges, or the gloves, or nothing at all. The day will resume its plain little duties. Somewhere a spoon will fall. Somewhere a person will laugh incorrectly. Somewhere a blue cup will break at last.

But later, Sarah—much later—you will understand that to remember is not to keep the past.

It is to be kept by it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal bedtime-story fragment with no quotation marks, simple sentences, and a quietly tragic tone, where a narrator speaks with a cigar-puffing sad-eyed man whose head is locked in a Japanese box.
counterfactuals.output:
The moon was thin as a fingernail clipping.

I found the sad-eyed man beside the nursery window. His head was locked in a Japanese box. The box was lacquered black, with cranes on the sides and a little brass moon over the latch. Smoke curled from a small hole near his mouth.

He puffed his cigar very slowly.

I asked him if it hurt.

He said it did not hurt anymore. He said the hurting had become a room he lived in. His voice was soft inside the box. It sounded like rain falling in a cupboard.

The wallpaper breathed around us. The sheep on the blanket lifted their woolly heads and watched. Far away, under the bed, a train went by with no passengers.

I asked him who had locked him there.

He looked at me with his wet brown eyes through the narrow slit.

He said a girl once kept her wishes in the box. Then she grew older and put him there instead. She forgot where she left the key.

He puffed again. The smoke made a little ladder to the ceiling. No one climbed it.

I told him I would look for the key in the morning.

He smiled sadly.

He said morning was a country that did not open for everyone.

Then the stars began to fall into the washbasin one by one. Each made a tiny silver sound. The sad-eyed man closed his eyes inside the Japanese box, and the cigar glowed like the last light in a house where nobody was coming home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
